q: Electric current through a conductor is defined as the:
o: Product of charge and time, I = Qt
Rate of flow of charge, I = Q/t
Charge per unit volume of the conductor
x: Current is the charge passing a cross-section per unit time, I = Q/t. Energy per unit charge is potential difference or emf, not current.

q: In 2 seconds, 5 × 10¹⁸ electrons flow through a cross-section of a conductor. What current does this represent? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
x: Q = ne = 5 × 10¹⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.8 C. I = Q/t = 0.8 ÷ 2 = 0.4 A. 0.8 A forgets to divide by the time.

q: Electric current has a direction, yet it is treated as a scalar quantity because:
o: It always flows in a straight line
Its direction is always from negative to positive
Currents add by ordinary arithmetic, not by the laws of vector addition
x: Currents meeting at a junction simply add as numbers, whatever the angles between the wires, so current does not obey vector addition and is a scalar.

q: In a pure semiconductor such as silicon, the electric current is carried by:
x: In a semiconductor, freed electrons move one way and the holes they leave behind move the other way; both carry current. Ions carry current in electrolytes.

q: Three lamps are connected in series to a battery, and a steady current flows. The current is:
o: Largest in the lamp nearest the positive terminal
The same at every point of the circuit
Smallest in the last lamp, because it is used up
x: In a steady current charge is not used up or stored anywhere, so the same charge passes every cross-section of a series circuit per second.

q: Electrons drift through a wire at only about a millimetre per second, yet a lamp lights almost the moment it is switched on. This is because:
o: Electrons travel from the switch to the lamp at the speed of light
The lamp stores electrons until it is switched on
The electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, so electrons everywhere start drifting together
Current flows only in the lamp and not in the wires
x: Switching on sets up the electric field along the whole circuit at nearly the speed of light, so free electrons already in the lamp filament start moving at once.

q: A steady current of 0.8 A flows through a lamp for 5 minutes. The number of electrons that pass through it is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):
x: Q = It = 0.8 × 300 = 240 C. n = Q/e = 240 ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5 × 10²¹. Using 5 s instead of 300 s gives 2.5 × 10¹⁹.

q: A conductor whose current is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant temperature, is called:
x: A conductor that obeys Ohm's law (I ∝ V at constant physical conditions) is called ohmic, for example a metal wire at steady temperature.

q: A resistor carries 2 A when 10 V is applied across it. If the voltage is raised to 25 V at the same temperature, the current becomes:
x: R = V/I = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 Ω, which stays the same. New current = 25 ÷ 5 = 5 A.

q: A filament lamp and a diode are non-ohmic devices. Plotted as current against voltage, their characteristic graphs are:
o: Curves, not straight lines through the origin
x: Ohmic devices give a straight line through the origin because V/I is constant. For non-ohmic devices, such as a diode or filament lamp, V/I changes, so the graph curves.

q: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a 6 Ω resistor. The power dissipated in it is:
x: Current I = V/R = 2 A. Power = VI = 12 × 2 = 24 W (or V²/R = 144 ÷ 6). 72 W comes from multiplying V by R.

q: Resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are joined in series across a 20 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The potential difference across the 6 Ω resistor is:
x: Total resistance = 10 Ω, so I = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 A. V across 6 Ω = 2 × 6 = 12 V; the 4 Ω resistor takes the other 8 V.

q: A lamp draws a current of 0.25 A from a 230 V supply. Its resistance while working is:
x: R = V/I = 230 ÷ 0.25 = 920 Ω. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 57.5.

q: An 18 V battery (no internal resistance) feeds a network: a 6 Ω resistor followed by a pair of 6 Ω resistors joined side by side. How much current leaves the battery?
x: The parallel pair is 3 Ω, so the total is 3 + 6 = 9 Ω. I = 18 ÷ 9 = 2 A. Adding all three as 18 Ω gives 1 A.

q: The resistivity ρ of the material of a wire of resistance R, length L and cross-sectional area A is given by:
x: From R = ρL/A, rearranging gives ρ = RA/L, which is why the unit of resistivity is Ω m.

q: A uniform wire is cut into two equal halves. Compared with the original wire, the resistivity of each half is:
x: Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature, not on size. Each half has half the resistance, but the same resistivity.

q: Wire P has length L and cross-sectional area A. Wire Q, of the same metal at the same temperature, has length 2L and area 2A. Compared with P, the resistance of Q is:
x: R = ρL/A. Doubling L doubles R and doubling A halves it, so the two effects cancel and the resistance is unchanged.

q: A wire of resistance 8 Ω is folded exactly in half and the two halves are twisted together to form a thicker wire. Its new resistance is:
x: Folding halves the length (R halves) and doubles the cross-sectional area (R halves again), so R becomes 8 ÷ 4 = 2 Ω.

q: The resistance of a semiconductor such as a thermistor decreases as its temperature rises because:
o: Its free electrons collide more often with atoms
More charge carriers are set free at higher temperature
x: Heating releases many more free electrons (and holes) in a semiconductor; this rise in charge carriers outweighs the extra collisions, so resistance falls.

q: For a metal wire, a graph of resistance against temperature in °C over the normal range is:
o: A straight line rising with temperature that does not pass through the origin
A straight line through the origin
x: R = R₀(1 + αt): R rises linearly with t and equals R₀ (not zero) at 0 °C, so the line has an intercept and does not pass through the origin.

q: The resistance of a wire is 5 Ω at 0 °C and 6 Ω at 100 °C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of its material is:
x: α = (R − R₀) ÷ (R₀ t) = (6 − 5) ÷ (5 × 100) = 1/500 = 2 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹. Dividing by 6 instead of 5 gives about 1.7 × 10⁻³.

q: The internal resistance of a cell is the resistance offered by:
o: The connecting wires of the external circuit
The load connected to the cell
The voltmeter connected across the cell
The electrolyte and electrodes inside the cell
x: Charges flowing through the cell itself meet resistance from its electrolyte and electrodes; this is the internal resistance r.

q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor. The current in the circuit is:
x: I = E ÷ (R + r) = 2 ÷ (3.5 + 0.5) = 0.5 A. Ignoring r gives 0.57 A.

q: A battery is being charged, so current is driven through it opposite to its normal direction. Its terminal potential difference V is:
o: Less than its emf, V = E − Ir
Equal to its emf at all currents
Greater than its emf, V = E + Ir
x: When charging, the charger must supply the emf plus the drop across the internal resistance, so V = E + Ir, larger than the emf.

q: A cell of internal resistance 2 Ω delivers a current of 0.5 A to an external circuit. The 'lost volts' inside the cell are:
x: Lost volts = Ir = 0.5 × 2 = 1 V, the difference between the emf and the terminal potential difference.

q: A battery of emf 12 V gives a terminal potential difference of 10 V while supplying 2 A to a resistor. The resistance of the external resistor is:
x: The external resistor has the terminal p.d. across it: R = V/I = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 Ω. Using the emf gives 6 Ω; 1 Ω is the internal resistance.

q: Two identical cells, each of emf E and internal resistance r, are connected in series (positive to negative). The combination has:
o: Emf E and internal resistance r/2
x: In series the emfs add and the internal resistances also add, giving 2E and 2r. Parallel identical cells would give E and r/2.

q: A cell drives a current of 1 A through a 4 Ω resistor and 0.5 A through a 10 Ω resistor. The emf of the cell is:
x: E = I(R + r): E = 1(4 + r) and E = 0.5(10 + r). So 4 + r = 5 + 0.5r, giving r = 2 Ω and E = 6 V.

q: The greatest power that a source of emf E and internal resistance r can deliver to an external load is:
x: Maximum power transfer occurs when R = r. Then I = E/2r and P = I²R = (E²/4r²) × r = E²/4r.

q: When a battery is matched to its load for the greatest power output, how large is the circuit current in terms of emf E and internal resistance r?
x: For maximum power R = r, so the total resistance is 2r and I = E/2r. E/r would be the short-circuit current.

q: A source with internal resistance 4 Ω delivers its greatest possible power, 9 W, to a matched load. The emf of the source is:
x: Maximum power = E²/4r, so E² = 4 × 4 × 9 = 144 and E = 12 V. Using E²/r gives 6 V.

q: Power stations and large batteries are not usually run under the maximum power transfer condition because:
o: The efficiency would be only 50%, so half the energy would be wasted in the source
The load would receive no power at all
The emf of the source would double
x: At R = r equal power is lost inside the source and delivered to the load, so efficiency is only 50%. Where efficiency matters, R is made much larger than r.

q: When the load resistance R is made much larger than the internal resistance r of a source, the efficiency of power transfer:
o: Approaches 100%, though the power delivered becomes small
Is the same as at maximum power transfer
x: Efficiency = R/(R + r), which approaches 1 when R ≫ r. But the current, and so the power, falls as R becomes very large.

q: A source of emf 6 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is first connected to a 1 Ω load and then to a 2 Ω load. The power in the load:
x: With 1 Ω: I = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A, P = 2² × 1 = 4 W. With 2 Ω: I = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 A, P = 1.5² × 2 = 4.5 W, the maximum, since R now equals r.

q: A source of internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 3 Ω load. The efficiency of power transfer to the load is:
x: Efficiency = R ÷ (R + r) = 3 ÷ 4 = 75%. The other 25% is dissipated inside the source; 50% applies only when R = r.
